one_liner: Alexandrescu's 2001 policy-based std::basic_string clone; only evidence is an anecdotal 5-10% Boost.Wave speedup.
what_it_does: flex_string<E, Traits, Alloc, Storage> re-implements the C++03 std::basic_string interface on top of a pluggable storage policy, so one typedef swaps the string type in existing code. Shipped policies are SimpleStringStorage (malloc/realloc), AllocatorStringStorage (the default, std::allocator), VectorStringStorage (wraps std::vector), SmallStringOpt<Storage, N> (in-object buffer up to 126 chars) and CowStringOpt<Storage> (reference-counted copy-on-write). The repo is a GitHub mirror of the SourceForge Loki library; flex_string is a set of headers under include/loki/flex/.
how_it_is_fast: There is no single algorithmic trick: the speed argument is that you pick the storage layout per workload. SimpleStringStorage grows with realloc (can extend in place, which std::allocator cannot), SmallStringOpt avoids heap allocation for short strings, and CowStringOpt makes copies O(1) by sharing a buffer whose reference count is stored in the buffer's first character. Character moves use memcpy/memmove and fills use a Duff's-device loop (flex_string_details.h). Boost.Wave's reported gain came from its default CowString<AllocatorStringStorage<char>> configuration, i.e. cheap copies of token strings.
when_to_use: Maintaining legacy C++03 code (or Boost.Wave-era code) that already uses flex_string and you need to understand or tune its storage policy.
Copy-heavy, single-threaded workloads such as token or symbol strings that are copied far more often than mutated, where a COW policy saves allocations.
Studying or teaching policy-based design: each storage policy is a few hundred lines and the interface contract is documented at the top of every policy header.
Experiments that need a custom string layout (arena-backed, fixed-size SSO threshold, malloc/realloc growth) without writing the full basic_string surface yourself.
when_not_to_use: Any new C++11-or-later code: flex_string has no move constructor or move assignment, so std::move, vector<flex_string> reallocation and swaps through generic code fall back to deep copies (or refcount traffic) where std::string moves in O(1).

C++20 builds with std::allocator: the Loki copy reads A::reference, A::pointer, A::const_pointer and calls A::allocate(n, hint), all removed in C++20; Boost.Wave had to patch exactly this (boostorg/wave PR #72, 2020) and the Loki mirror has not changed since 2013.

Strings shared across threads with CowStringOpt: the reference count is a plain unsigned char/short in the buffer, incremented and decremented without atomics, so concurrent copies of one string are a data race.

Workloads built from many small appends (s += "ab" in a loop): Storage::append reserves exactly size()+n, so with the default AllocatorStringStorage every append that overflows reallocates and copies the whole string (quadratic); only push_back doubles capacity.

Search-heavy code: find(const char*, pos, n) calls traits::compare at every position and find(char) is implemented as a 1-character compare per position, with no memchr first-character skip as in libstdc++.

integration.dependencies: none (the rest of Loki needs src/*.cpp for SmallObj, Singleton and OrderedStatic, but flex_string does not)
integration.min_toolchain: C++03; README lists GCC 3.4-4.1 and MSVC 7.1/8.0; the Loki copy does not compile as C++20 with std::allocator (removed allocator members)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Separate strings are independent; CowStringOpt shares buffers with a non-atomic in-buffer reference count, and c_str() (a const member) writes the terminating zero into the buffer, so concurrent const access is formally a data race.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — C++03 std::basic_string interface only: no move semantics, none of the C++11 members (pop_back, front, back, shrink_to_fit), data() is not guaranteed null-terminated (only c_str() writes the terminator), and const at(n) accepts n == size() instead of throwing.

gotchas: CowStringOpt keeps the reference count in the first element of the buffer, typed as the unsigned variant of the character type (unsigned char for char), so after 255 sharers a copy silently becomes a deep copy; the count is not atomic.
data() returns the buffer without writing a terminator; only c_str() writes E() at pEnd_, so passing data() to C APIs reads whatever byte follows the string.

AllocatorStringStorage computes its allocation in bytes and passes byte counts to A::allocate(1 + (sz-1)/sizeof(E)) but A::deallocate(p, bytes), which mismatches for wchar_t under sized deallocation; Boost.Wave also hit gcc 11 -Wfree-nonheap-object warnings on the shared emptyString_ sentinel (boostorg/wave issue #159).
The SmallStringOpt threshold is capped at 126 characters by a compile-time check, and its size/flag byte lives in the last buffer slot, so sizeof(flex_string) grows with the threshold.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you specifically want a C++03 policy-based string (COW, realloc growth or tunable SSO behind one interface); FastString and MengRao/str have measured wins over a modern std::string with numbers you can reproduce, and buffet or to_static_string cover the narrower append and number-formatting cases.
verified_claims_summary: The only number is second-hand: Hartmut Kaiser told the author that dropping flex_string (in Boost.Wave's default copy-on-write configuration) into the Boost.Wave preprocessor made it 5-10% faster depending on input, against an unstated 2001-2005 era std::string, with no compiler, hardware or benchmark code; the doc page itself says no performance comparison suite exists, and the repo's test/flex_string/main.cpp is a randomized correctness comparison against std::string with no timing.
status_note: Abandoned since 2013 (last mirror commit 2013-08-06, README last updated 2005, one open unrelated issue); permissively licensed (Alexandrescu notice, Loki MIT, BSL-1.0 copy in Boost.Wave) and small enough to vendor, but the maintained copy is Boost.Wave's boost/wave/util/flex_string.hpp, which carries C++20 and warning fixes the Loki mirror lacks.
